rationale: The only governing-law/venue provision (§ 20(h)) selects the laws of Nova Scotia (and Canadian law applicable there) with the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the Nova Scotia courts. Nova Scotia is not among the accepted laws (New York, Delaware, California, or England and Wales), so the clause fails the fallback on both material terms (governing law and forum). It is not walk-away territory: the forum is our own home province (Sparkling is in Dartmouth, NS, while Garman is in Saskatoon, SK), the jurisdiction grant is non-exclusive, and there is no arbitration provision anywhere in the agreement. Redline moves the clause to the preferred position (New York law, exclusive New York County courts) while leaving the rest of the sentence structure intact; Delaware, California, or England and Wales/London remains available as a fallback if Garman pushes back.

Noted but not disqualifying: the displaced forum is our client's own home province and the grant was non-exclusive, so the practical benefit of the change is modest; the rationale already flags this and correctly declines to treat it as walk-away (walk-away is keyed to the vendor's home jurisdiction plus exclusive foreign venue or foreign-seated arbitration). Under a parametric rule with an enumerated accepted set, Nova Scotia remains a deviation. Deterministic checks all pass: the operation applies, the substituted law is within the accepted set, and the edit is scoped to the single governing-law paragraph.

quote: Sparkling shall pay the fees as set out in the Fee Schedule in accordance with the terms of this Agreement and the Fee Schedule.
rationale: No most-favoured-nation or most-favoured-customer language appears anywhere in the Agreement. Searches for "most favoured/favorable", "no less favourable", "other customers", "lowest", "price" and "any third party" returned nothing of the kind, and the fee and maintenance provisions (Section 11 fees, Section 10 maintenance at Fee Schedule rates) simply oblige Sparkling to pay scheduled fees without any commitment to extend Garman terms given to third parties or to match third-party offers. This meets the preferred position (no MFN obligation on the Customer), so no redline is warranted. Note only that the Agreement likewise contains no MFN running in our favour, which we could raise commercially if better pricing benchmarking is desired.

quote: Sparkling shall pay the fees as set out in the Fee Schedule in accordance with the terms of this Agreement and the Fee Schedule.
rationale: The Agreement contains no minimum purchase commitment, take-or-pay, shortfall charge or volume cap on us. Searches for "minimum", "commit", "shortfall", "take or pay", "non-cancellable" and "volume" return nothing relevant (the only "commitment" hit, p0143, is the no-agency clause). Fees are payable only as set out in the Fee Schedule (§11/p0084), with additional fees arising only if we choose to use the Software beyond the Authorized Locations (§2/p0028). Maintenance runs in a renewable one-year term rather than a fixed multi-year obligation (§10/p0065), and we may terminate the whole Agreement for convenience on ninety (90) days' notice (§17(b)/p0118), so there is no locked-in spend without an exit. This meets the preferred position (fees for usage or ordered services only). Note: the commercial exposure sits in Schedule "A" (Fee Schedule), which is not reproduced in this text — worth confirming the schedule itself carries no committed user/location counts or minimum annual maintenance spend.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] We cannot accept a no-hire covering all of the other party's employees. We have narrowed this to a mutual non-solicitation limited to personnel directly involved in the services for 12 months after their involvement ends, with the customary carve-outs for general advertising and unsolicited approaches.

ops.newText: During the term of this Agreement and for a period of twelve (12) months following the end of an individual's involvement in the provision of services under this Agreement, neither party shall, and neither party shall permit its affiliates to, directly solicit for employment any employee of the other party who was directly involved in the provision of services under this Agreement. This Section does not prohibit either party from hiring any person, and does not apply to general advertisements or other recruitment activity not specifically targeted at the other party's personnel, or to any person who approaches a party on his or her own initiative.
ops.oldText: During the term of this Agreement and for a period of one year thereafter, both parties agree not to hire or allow its respective affiliates to hire any employee of the other party, or any person who was an employee of the other party during the previous six months and who was directly involved in the provision of services under this Agreement.

proposal.summary: Convert the mutual no-hire into a narrow 12-month non-solicit limited to personnel directly involved in the services, with general-advertising and unsolicited-approach carve-outs.

quote: During the term of this Agreement and for a period of one year thereafter, both parties agree not to hire or allow its respective affiliates to hire any employee of the other party, or any person who was an employee of the other party during the previous six months and who was directly involved in the provision of services under this Agreement.
rationale: Section 19 binds us as Customer and is a no-hire, not a non-solicit ("agree not to hire or allow its respective affiliates to hire"). Its first limb reaches "any employee of the other party" without any connection to the engagement, and the "directly involved" qualifier attaches only to the second (former-employee) limb. There is no carve-out for general advertising or unsolicited approaches. A no-hire covering all Vendor personnel is walk-away territory under this rule, so the clause fails the fallback on material terms notwithstanding that it is mutual and only one year long. We have narrowed it with minimal edits to the fallback position: a mutual non-solicit limited to personnel directly involved in the services, 12 months from the end of that involvement, with express general-advertising and unsolicited-approach carve-outs and deletion of the no-hire. Survival via Section 18 is acceptable once the covenant is narrowed.

The redline reaches the fallback precisely: mutual, limited to personnel directly involved in the services, 12 months measured from the end of that involvement, express carve-outs for general advertisements/non-targeted recruitment and self-initiated approaches, and deletion of the no-hire (with a clarifying sentence that hiring is not prohibited). The failed 'minimal edit' heuristic (0.753 changed-character ratio) is justified here: converting a no-hire into a narrowed non-solicit and adding the required carve-out sentence cannot be done without rewriting the clause; no extraneous terms were introduced. quote: For a renewable one-year term commencing upon the Maintenance Commencement Date, subject to payment of maintenance fees in accordance with the Fee Schedule but without additional fees or charges, Garman shall provide the following Maintenance Services:
rationale:
Compliant at the preferred position; no redline and no counterparty comment.

(1) No auto-renewal exists. Searches for "automatically renew" return nothing; the only renewal reference is p0065, under which maintenance runs "For a renewable one-year term" — a 12-month term extendable only by the parties' affirmative agreement. The licence itself "shall remain in effect perpetually as long as fees are paid" (p0117). There is therefore no rolling term, no multi-year renewal, and no "unless notice ... days prior" condition to compute. This is the preferred position: renewal by mutual agreement on a 12-month term.

(2) The ninety-day figure is not a non-renewal notice window. It appears only in p0118 — "Sparkling may terminate this Agreement at any time upon ninety (90) calendar days written notice to Garman" — which is our own termination-for-convenience right. It binds Garman to accept our exit, benefits our party, and is not a condition on renewal, so it is excluded from the ≤60-day parameter and belongs to a termination rule instead.

(3) Minor sub-elements short of ideal drafting, noted not flagged: no CPI/3% cap on renewal-period maintenance fee uplift (fees are simply "in accordance with the Fee Schedule") and no 60-day vendor renewal reminder. Per the classification semantics these are not deviations; we would raise the uplift cap in the Fee Schedule negotiation rather than by redlining Section 10.

verification.notes: non-renewal notice window ≤ 60 days: value=90 Claimed status is compliant with no redline and no counterparty comment, which is the expected output shape; the rendered paragraphs are identical to the originals. The cited text supports compliance: p0065 provides a 'renewable one-year term' with no 'automatically renew' language and no 'unless notice … days prior' condition, and p0117 makes the licence perpetual subject to fee payment — i.e., no rolling or multi-year renewal to exit. The failed deterministic check (value=90) is a false positive: the ninety-day figure in p0118 is Sparkling's (our) termination-for-convenience notice, a right that benefits our party and is not a non-renewal notice window, so it falls outside the ≤60-day parameter. The absent CPI/3% uplift cap and 60-day vendor reminder are correctly treated as minor sub-elements noted in the rationale rather than flagged as deviations, consistent with the classification semantics.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] Section 17(b) requires us to return or destroy Garman's Software, but nothing obliges Garman to hand back our data or help us move off the system, so we have added a reciprocal exit provision. Our playbook position is up to six months of transition assistance at then-current rates, return of our data within thirty days in a machine-readable format and certified deletion thereafter; we can accept ninety days of assistance if that suits Garman better.

ops.text: (d) Upon expiry or termination of this Agreement for any reason, Garman shall (i) at Sparkling's request, provide reasonable transition assistance for a period of up to six (6) months at Garman's then-current rates; (ii) within thirty (30) calendar days of such expiry or termination, return to Sparkling all of Sparkling's data and Confidential Information in Garman's possession or control, in a commonly used, machine-readable format; and (iii) thereafter delete or destroy all such data and Confidential Information remaining in its systems and certify such deletion in writing to Sparkling.

proposal.summary: Insert Section 17(d) requiring Garman to provide up to six months' transition assistance, return Sparkling's data within 30 days in machine-readable format, and certify deletion thereafter.

quote: Sparkling shall cease using the Software at the end of the ninety (90) day notice period, and shall certify to Garman within thirty (30) calendar days of termination that Sparkling has destroyed or has returned to Garman all Software, Documentation and Codes.
rationale: Section 17 (Term and Termination) imposes exit obligations only on us — cease use of the Software and certify destruction/return of Software, Documentation and Codes — with no reciprocal obligation on Garman. There is no transition-assistance, data-export or deletion-certification provision anywhere: Section 8(b) returns our Confidential Information only in the narrow rejection-of-Software scenario, Section 4 covers data conversion at implementation, Section 16 escrow only releases source code, Section 14 has no return-on-termination mechanic, and Section 18 survival adds nothing on point. The rule's fallback (90 days' assistance plus 30-day export) is therefore also unmet, so we insert a new Section 17(d) at the preferred position: up to six months' assistance at then-current rates, return of our data within thirty days in a machine-readable format, and certified deletion thereafter.
ruleTitle: Post-termination transition assistance and data return

verification.notes: The rule is a 'missing'-kind insert and the rationale credibly surveys the candidate clauses (Sections 4, 8(b), 14, 16, 17, 18) showing exit obligations run only against us (cease use, certify destruction of Software) with no reciprocal data-return, transition-assistance or deletion-certification mechanic, so neither the preferred nor the fallback position is met. The inserted Section 17(d) tracks the playbook model language closely (up to six months' assistance at then-current rates, return of data within thirty days in a machine-readable format, then deletion with written certification) and is placed at the end of the Term and Termination section, which is the location the redline guidance specifies; subsection lettering (d) follows the existing (b)/(c) sequence. The insert is additive only — no existing text is altered or deleted — so the edit is the smallest change that reaches the playbook position; the modest extension to Confidential Information alongside data is consistent with the rule's intent and does not create a directional problem for us. Comment is accurate (correctly characterises the one-sided Section 17(b) obligation), concise, in first person plural with the required prefix, states the playbook position and offers the 90-day fallback, matching tone requirements. Deterministic checks both pass and are consistent with the substance of the insert.

quote: For the acceptance period and for a period of one year from the Maintenance Commencement Date, and thereafter for as long as the Software is covered by Maintenance Services and is used by Sparkling in accordance with this Agreement, Garman warrants that the Software shall perform in conformance with the Specifications in all material respects.
rationale: Section 12 gives an express conformance warranty running through the acceptance period, a full year from the Maintenance Commencement Date and thereafter for as long as Maintenance Services continue — at or above the preferred 12-month software warranty. A real remedy exists: Garman must repair non-conforming Software at no charge under the Software Repair Service (§10(c)/p0077), and a full refund of all amounts paid is available if the Software is rejected on acceptance (§8(b)). Critically, there is no "AS IS" or implied-warranty disclaimer anywhere in the agreement, so nothing swallows the express warranty, and §15 preserves direct damages. Sub-elements short of the preferred wording — no separate professional-and-workmanlike services warranty, no express compliance-with-laws or no-malicious-code warranties, and repair rather than an express repair/replace/refund election — are noted but are not material deviations given the longer-than-preferred period and the refund path on rejection. No redline proposed.

Shortfalls versus the preferred wording (no separate professional-and-workmanlike services warranty, no compliance-with-laws or no-malicious-code warranties, 'best efforts to repair' rather than an express repair/replace/refund election) are correctly treated as sub-elements noted in the rationale rather than flagged deviations, consistent with the playbook's classification semantics.
